title: Sword and pen
hookLine: a warrior who was also a poet, in the same hand

cards: A hand that has held a bowstring all afternoon picks up a pen at night. The fingers are sore. There's a battle behind and probably another ahead.
And the pen moves anyway: praise of the Timeless One, a story of his own life, a ballad, a letter to an emperor. Today, step back from the writings of Guru Gobind Singh and look at the hand itself.

teach.b: Sikhs have a name for this pairing: sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier. A sant is a person of devotion. A sipahi is a soldier.
The ideal is one person who is both at once, not a soldier on weekdays and a saint on holy days. Think back over the block. The Bachitar Natak tells of battle in verse.
The Zafarnama is a letter of rebuke, but it opens with praise of God. And a verse from a composition in the Dasam Granth gathers the two halves into a single plea.

teach.h: PRAISE AND BATTLE IN ONE BLOCK.
teach.b: Paraphrased, as Sikhs read it, it asks God for a gift: that I never turn away from doing good; that when I go out to face the enemy I have no fear and win; that I teach my own mind to long for Your praise; and that when my time comes, I die fighting in the thick of battle.

teach.h: NEVER TURN AWAY FROM DOING GOOD.
teach.b: Doing good comes first. Courage follows. The mind's longing for praise sits in the middle.
Only then the sword. The fighting is for something, and the something is written first. The pairing is still there in Sikh life.
A Khalsa Sikh keeps the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, and may carry a prayer book, a gutka, close by too. Neither cancels the other.
In this reading, the pen without the sword could be words with no backbone; the sword without the pen, strength with no reason. He kept them in one hand.

how: Khalsa Sikhs keep the kirpan as an article of faith alongside daily prayer, and the ideal of the sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier, is taught in gurdwaras and Sikh homes.

o: a scholar who writes about well-known old battles
devotion and courage held together in one life
a soldier who gives up fighting to pray instead

games.q: pen and sword: tap the pairs.
p: a small sword, an article of faith

s: the saint-soldier is a saint on holy days and a soldier on others
the ideal is one person who is both at once.
in the verse, doing good comes before the battle
it asks first never to turn away from doing good; the battle comes last.
the Zafarnama is pure rebuke with no praise
it opens with praise of God.

games.q: you're asking God for one gift before a fight. what does the Tenth Guru's verse ask for first?
o: never to turn away from doing good.
games.why: doing good comes first, then courage and the longing for praise, and only last the battle.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you'd stand up for even when it costs you, a person, a principle, a place, and find two or four plain lines about it, no rhyme needed.
Write them down or say them over in your head, and notice which line feels strongest.

wordCard.voice: Sword and pen. Guru Gobind Singh as sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier: devotion and courage held by one person, with doing good written first. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: saint-soldier, the Sikh ideal of devotion and courage in one person.

carryVoice: Your line: pen and sword. A saint and a soldier, in one person. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandi Charitar (Dasam Granth), the verse beginning deh shiva bar mohe ihai, paraphrased
